<reason>PRO built a tight two-part case (unreliability plus weak prediction) and then systematically narrowed the debate: CON barely defended hiring, and when pressed gave a "yes, narrowly" answer that PRO turned into "a rounding error picks someone's first manager." PRO's reform-equals-Big-Five argument was never really dislodged; CON's "same product, read the scores" reply doesn't explain what remains distinctively MBTI/DISC beyond the letters. CON's best material was the burden asymmetry ("one defensible room") and the non-evaluative-frame idea, but PRO's closing landed cleanly on CON's own line—"the letters open the conversation; the specifics carry it"—showing the value sits in the non-MBTI part and the defect in the MBTI part, and framed "every dimension is legitimate" as conceding the instrument measures nothing. CON's "replaceability isn't the motion" is a fair point but doesn't rescue the labels' accuracy claim. PRO had a small execution blemish (nonexistent [C1.x] reference IDs), but otherwise made the decision easier: hiring conceded, reform collapses into Big Five, team-building value survives without the typology.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's closing seizing CON's "letters open the conversation; the specifics carry it" and CON's "no dimension is a verdict" frame, arguing CON located the benefit in what isn't the product and the flaw in what is—plus turning CON's "yes, narrowly" hiring answer into a decision moved by an invalid score.</best_rebuttal>
